references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Some use and development is exempt under clause 4 of the Tasmanian Planning Scheme. Each zone table classes the use classes as No Permit Required, Permitted, Discretionary or Prohibited. Planning approval is needed for Permitted or Discretionary use and development. A Permitted application that relies only on Acceptable Solutions must be approved and is not advertised. Discretionary applications rely on Performance Criteria. Councils decide Permitted applications within 28 days and Discretionary within 42 days; the clock stops while further information is provided, and may be longer where Heritage Tasmania or the EPA is involved.

Requests for more information must be made within 14 days (Permitted) or 21 days (Discretionary). The assessment clock starts once the invoice is paid. A permit lapses after 2 years if not substantially commenced, and council can grant two 2-year extensions.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Building work has four categories. Category 1 low risk work can be done by the owner or a competent person without a permit. Category 2 low risk work must be done by a licensed builder, with no approval but compliance with the National Construction Code. Category 3 notifiable work needs licensed designers and builders and a building surveyor's Certificate of Likely Compliance before work starts. Category 4 permit work needs a Certificate of Likely Compliance and a building or demolition permit from the council's permit authority. Plumbing work follows the same four categories; notifiable plumbing needs a Certificate of Likely Compliance from the permit authority and permit plumbing also needs a plumbing permit. Each of the 29 councils has a permit authority.
references.interpretation: New houses, granny flats and most extensions are notifiable or permit work, so a building surveyor's certificate is likely. Captured on 2026-10-12 from an automated summary of the published page; the exact wording was not available. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] For permit work the building surveyor issues a certificate of likely compliance within 21 days, which expires after 12 months. The permit authority must deal with the building permit application within 7 days or an agreed period. The builder lodges a start work notice and must not begin until the building surveyor's start work authorisation. Mandatory notification stages are inspected within one day of notice. At completion, the owner applies to the permit authority for a certificate of completion with the occupancy permit issued by the building surveyor. Owners must not allow occupation until an occupancy permit is issued where one is required. The Building Administration Fee and the Building and Construction Industry Training levy are payable where the work is worth over $20,000. Permit plumbing work gets a certificate of likely compliance within 21 days and a plumbing permit from the permit authority.

references.section: Planning and building in bushfire-prone areas
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] New development in a bushfire-prone area needs a bushfire hazard management plan unless an exemption applies, usually at the building stage, and the Tasmania Fire Service recommends including it with any planning application. Land within 100 m of bushfire-prone vegetation is treated as bushfire-prone where there is no overlay. A TFS-accredited bushfire hazard practitioner sets the bushfire attack level (BAL) and prepares the plan. Building must meet AS 3959. Private access needs a carriageway at least 4 m wide and a reliable firefighting water supply.
references.interpretation: Bushfire-prone land adds a bushfire hazard management plan and BAL construction. rule_sets.title: Tasmania: houses, extensions and granny flats
rule_sets.description: Planning permit, certificate of likely compliance, building and plumbing permits and occupancy for new houses, extensions and secondary residences in Tasmania.
limitations: We don't know your zone or which codes apply to your land, so we can't say whether your project is exempt, no permit required, permitted or discretionary.
The Tasmanian Planning Scheme's zone and code rules are not encoded. The LIST map (LISTmap) shows your zone and code overlays.
Constraints like heritage, bushfire, flooding and landslip come from your answers. Not ticking one doesn't mean it doesn't apply.
Not legal advice. Confirm with your council, a building surveyor or a town planner before you rely on it.

rules.title: A planning permit may be needed, depending on zone and codes
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified. MAY_APPLY because we don't know the zone, codes or design.

outcomes.title: You may need a planning permit
outcomes.detail: In Tasmania the Tasmanian Planning Scheme decides whether your project is exempt, no permit required, permitted or discretionary. A house that meets every acceptable solution in a residential zone may need no permit or be permitted, decided in 28 days. If it relies on performance criteria it is discretionary: it is advertised for 14 days and decided in 42 days. Look up your zone and codes on the LIST map, then ask your council.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under the Land Use Planning and Approvals Act 1993, assessed against the Tasmanian Planning Scheme

evidence.title: Site plan with setbacks, heights and existing buildings
Current title search with folio plan and any schedule of easements

payload.task: Look up your zone and code overlays on the LIST map and ask council whether you need a planning permit

rules.title: Building work needs a building surveyor's certificate
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified. Some small extensions may be low risk work; LIKELY not REQUIRED.

outcomes.title: You likely need a certificate of likely compliance
outcomes.detail: A new house, granny flat or most extensions is notifiable or permit building work under the Building Act 2016. You engage a licensed building surveyor, who checks the plans against the National Construction Code and issues a certificate of likely compliance before work starts (within 21 days for permit work). Your designer supplies a Tasmanian Form 35 certificate of the responsible designer with the plans.

approval.authority: A licensed building surveyor you engage
approval.pathway: Certificate of likely compliance under the Building Act 2016 (notifiable or permit building work)

evidence.title: Design documents and the designer's certificate

rules.title: Permit building work needs a building permit
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified. Whether a typical new house is notifiable or permit work depends on the Director's Determination and wasn't confirmed; MAY_APPLY.

outcomes.title: You may need a building permit from council
outcomes.detail: If your building surveyor classes the work as permit work (category 4), you also need a building permit from your council's permit authority. The surveyor's certificate of likely compliance goes with the Tasmanian Form 2 building work application. Council must deal with it within 7 days or an agreed period. Levies apply where the work is worth over $20,000: 0.1% Building Permit Levy and 0.2% training levy.

approval.pathway: Building permit under the Building Act 2016 (permit building work)

payload.task: Ask your building surveyor whether the work is notifiable or permit work

rules.title: Plumbing for a new home
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: You likely need plumbing approval
outcomes.detail: New bathrooms, kitchens and sewer or stormwater connections are notifiable or permit plumbing work. A licensed plumber does the work and council's permit authority issues a certificate of likely compliance and, for permit work, a plumbing permit before work starts. Apply with the Tasmanian Form 3 plumbing work application. Plumbing fees are about $460 to $540 at many councils.

approval.pathway: Plumbing permit and certificate of likely compliance under the Building Act 2016

payload.task: Have your plumber or designer lodge the plumbing application with council

rules.title: Heritage-listed places
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified. 'Heritage listing' may be local only (planning scheme code), not the state register; LIKELY_REQUIRED kept because both need approval.

outcomes.title: Heritage listing means you likely need a planning permit and heritage approval
outcomes.detail: If your place is on the Tasmanian Heritage Register, works need a minor works approval or approval from the Tasmanian Heritage Council. Most go through a council development application that council refers to the Heritage Council, which can add time. If your place is in the planning scheme's Local Historic Heritage Code, council assesses it as part of your planning permit. Call Heritage Tasmania's free heritage advisers on 1300 850 332 first.

approval.pathway: Minor works approval or Heritage Council approval under the Historic Cultural Heritage Act 1995

evidence.title: Heritage impact statement for major works

payload.task: Call a Heritage Tasmania heritage adviser before you design

outcomes.title: A heritage code makes a planning permit likely
outcomes.detail: Work to a heritage place or in a heritage precinct is rarely exempt. Expect a planning permit, often discretionary, with 14 days of advertising and a 42-day decision.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under the Land Use Planning and Approvals Act 1993, assessed against the Tasmanian Planning Scheme

rules.title: Bushfire-prone areas
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: You'll need a bushfire hazard management plan
outcomes.detail: New buildings in bushfire-prone areas need a bushfire hazard management plan and a bushfire attack level (BAL) assessment by a Tasmania Fire Service accredited bushfire hazard practitioner, unless an exemption applies. It is usually needed for building approval, and should go with any planning application. Higher BALs mean more expensive construction to AS 3959.

evidence.title: Bushfire hazard management plan and BAL assessment

payload.task: Engage an accredited bushfire hazard practitioner

rules.title: Secondary residences up to 60 m2
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified. 60 m2 current; 90 m2 under SPP Amendment 01/2026, not in effect at 2026-10-12.

outcomes.title: At 60 m2 or less, it can be a secondary residence
outcomes.detail: Under the State Planning Provisions a secondary residence (granny flat) can be up to 60 m2 and must not have its own electricity, water or sewer connections. If your zone allows a single dwelling and the design meets every development standard, you may not need a planning permit, unless a code like heritage or flooding applies. You still need building and plumbing approval. A change to allow 90 m2 is proposed but not yet in effect.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under the Land Use Planning and Approvals Act 1993, assessed against the Tasmanian Planning Scheme (may be no permit required if every standard is met)

payload.task: Check your design against the secondary residence rules and ask council to confirm

outcomes.title: Over 60 m2, it isn't a secondary residence yet
outcomes.detail: Today a secondary residence can be no more than 60 m2. A larger one is treated as a second dwelling, which usually needs a discretionary planning permit and may not be allowed in your zone. SPP Amendment 01/2026 proposes 90 m2, but you can't apply on that basis until it takes effect.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under the Land Use Planning and Approvals Act 1993, assessed against the Tasmanian Planning Scheme (multiple dwellings)

payload.task: Reduce to 60 m2 or get planning advice on a second dwelling

rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Your granny flat would sit with your existing house
outcomes.detail: A secondary residence is an extra small dwelling on the same site as the main house, sharing its service connections.

outcomes.title: Without a house, it isn't a secondary residence
outcomes.detail: A secondary residence has to go with a main house on the same site. Build the house first or apply for both together, or get planning advice.

rules.title: Subdividing needs a planning permit
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified. Whether every subdivision is discretionary wasn't confirmed.

outcomes.title: You need a planning permit to subdivide
outcomes.detail: Subdivision needs a planning permit from council under the Tasmanian Planning Scheme. A registered land surveyor usually prepares the plan. Most subdivisions are discretionary: advertised for 14 days and decided in 42 days. Example fee: $959 plus $223 per lot at Kingborough Council in 2026-27.

approval.pathway: Planning permit under the Land Use Planning and Approvals Act 1993, assessed against the Tasmanian Planning Scheme

evidence.title: Proposed plan of subdivision from a registered land surveyor

rules.title: Sealing the final plan
rules.notes: Effective from the date the source was read (2026-10-12), not the date the law began: capped at likely until the reference is verified.

outcomes.title: Council must seal your final plan before new titles
outcomes.detail: Once the permit conditions and any works are done, your surveyor gives council the final plan of survey. Council seals it when conditions are met and fees are paid. The sealed plan is then lodged with the Land Titles Office to create the new titles. Budget for a public open space contribution (often about 5% of land value) and TasWater and engineering costs.

approval.authority: Your local council (seals the final plan), then the Land Titles Office (registers it)
approval.pathway: Sealing of the final plan under the Local Government (Building and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1993

payload.task: Budget for works, open space contribution and the sealing fee
